title: Governor of Massachusetts

context.text: Democratic Gov. Maura Healey is running for a second term.

In the September 1, 2026 primary, Healey was unopposed for the Democratic nomination. Michael Minogue, a former biotech executive, won the Republican nomination with 75.6% of the vote to Brian Shortsleeve's 24.1%.
Andrea James, an unenrolled (independent) candidate, is also on the ballot with running mate Kayla Kittredge.

Minogue's running mate, New Bedford city councilor Shawn Oliver, was arrested after a crash on Dartmouth Street in New Bedford late on Saturday, October 17, 2026. New Bedford police charged him with operating under the influence of alcohol, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, speeding and a marked-lanes violation, according to The New Bedford Light; these are charges, not findings. Oliver announced on October 18 that he was suspending his campaign, saying "This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters." Minogue asked him to suspend his campaign. The deadline to withdraw passed in September, so Oliver's name remains on the ballot beside Minogue's.

candidates.name: Maura Healey
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll. Unopposed in the September 1 Democratic primary.

summary.text: Maura Healey is the incumbent Governor of Massachusetts, seeking a second term with Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll. She was elected in 2022 after serving as Attorney General from 2015 to 2023. As governor she signed a 2024 law revising the state's firearm statutes, the 2024 Affordable Homes Act, and in August 2026 a bill removing restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks of gestation.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree from Harvard University and a J.D. from Northeastern University School of Law.

Worked in the Massachusetts Attorney General's office from 2007, where she led the Civil Rights Division and its challenge to the federal Defense of Marriage Act, and later headed the Public Protection and Advocacy Bureau and the Business and Labor Bureau.
Elected Massachusetts Attorney General in 2014 and re-elected in 2018, serving January 2015 to January 2023; elected governor in 2022.

priorities.text: Affordability: in the October 8 debate she argued that her administration has cut taxes, expanded housing, capped health care costs and made community college free, while President Trump's policies are pushing prices higher.
Housing production: she credits the law she filed and signed with bringing 100,000 homes online.
priorities.quote: we have 100,000 homes coming online because I filed and signed the strongest housing law in the country

positions.summary: Signed legislation (H.5595) in August 2026 removing the existing restrictions on abortions at or beyond 24 weeks and leaving the decision to the physician's professional judgment.

Signed a 2024 law that tightened oversight of unserialized 'ghost guns,' expanded the state's red-flag law, barred non-law-enforcement firearm possession at schools, polling places and government buildings, and set penalties for modification devices such as Glock switches.

Signed the 2024 Affordable Homes Act, which authorizes state financing for production and preservation of housing for low- and moderate-income residents and requires cities and towns to permit housing as of right on certain state-conveyed surplus land, and says 100,000 homes are coming online because of it.

record.text: Signed Chapter 135 of the Acts of 2024 (H.4885), a revision of the state's firearm laws.
Signed Chapter 150 of the Acts of 2024, the Affordable Homes Act, authorizing a housing capital program.

Signed H.5595 (Chapter 188 of the Acts of 2026), which removes restrictions on abortion after 24 weeks of gestation. The House voted 119-33 on July 22, 2026 to pass it to be engrossed and enacted it 121-35 on July 31; the Senate passed it to be engrossed on July 31 by a 15-4 standing vote.

candidates.name: Mike Minogue
candidates.ballotNote: Running mate Shawn Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor, suspended his campaign on October 18 but remains on the ballot. Won the September 1 Republican primary over Brian Shortsleeve.

summary.text: Mike Minogue is a former biotech executive who led the heart-pump maker Abiomed for nearly two decades and is a first-time candidate. He won the Republican nomination with 75.6% of the primary vote. His 'Blueprint for a Better Future' centers on accountability, affordability, opportunity and keeping communities safe, including audits of the Legislature and state budget, tax cuts, ending enforcement of the MBTA Communities Act and canceling the state's net-zero emissions mandate.

background.text: Army veteran who led Abiomed, a heart-pump and medical-device company, for nearly two decades; Johnson & Johnson acquired the company in 2022.
First-time candidate for public office; won about 70% of delegates at the April 2026 state Republican convention.

priorities.text: Accountability: auditing the state Legislature and the entire state budget with an outside auditor, and creating a 'Massachusetts Spending Dashboard.'
Affordability: cutting taxes, temporarily suspending the state gas tax when prices climb, and cutting state-mandated energy utility fees.
Keeping communities safe: protecting qualified immunity for law enforcement, ending cashless bail and not allowing Massachusetts to become a sanctuary state.

positions.summary: His blueprint says he would cancel the state's net-zero emissions mandate and instead focus on energy innovation to lower energy costs.
positions.quote: [c]ancel the unfunded, unachievable Net Zero mandate

positions.summary: He would end enforcement of the MBTA Communities Act's multifamily zoning requirement, which he calls an unfunded mandate, while proposing to let cities and towns keep more of their tax dollars if they expedite single-family home permitting.
Proposed expanding charter, technical and vocational schools statewide.
Says he would keep Massachusetts from becoming a 'sanctuary state' and crack down on undocumented immigrants.

candidates.name: Andrea James
candidates.ballotNote: Unenrolled candidate running with Kayla Kittredge. Initially filed to run as a Democrat and switched her party affiliation to unenrolled in November 2025.
candidates.currentRole: Founder and executive director, National Council for Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Women and Girls

summary.text: Andrea James is a former criminal defense attorney and advocate for incarcerated women and girls running as an independent. She spent two years in federal prison for wire fraud and was disbarred. In a statement on her website, she said people deserve affordable homes, good schools, universal child care, 'Medicare for All,' renewable energy and a 'public banking system that prioritizes people over profit.'

background.text: Founded Families for Justice as Healing and is founder and executive director of the National Council for Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Women and Girls.

priorities.text: Housing for All, universal health care and universal child care.
Ending state cooperation with ICE and protecting immigrant families.
priorities.quote: End State Cooperation with ICE & Protect Immigrant Families

positions.summary: Her platform lists affordable housing and rent stabilization under what Massachusetts can afford.
Her platform lists Medicare for All in Massachusetts.
Her platform lists universal child care.
Her platform calls for ending state cooperation with ICE and protecting immigrant families.
positions.quote: End State Cooperation with ICE & Protect Immigrant Families

positions.summary: Her platform lists a rapid transition to 100% clean energy.
positions.quote: Rapid, Just Transition to 100% Clean Energy

statements.context: Listed on her platform page under 'Massachusetts Can Afford'

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and priorities come from her campaign website's platform and home pages (list-style headings, not full policy papers). The platform lists a '$25 Living Wage' without saying whether that is a minimum wage, so it is shown as a statement. No statements on abortion, guns or taxes were found.

researchNotes: Running mates are noted in each candidate's ballotNote rather than as separate entries. Ballotpedia was not reachable (it blocks automated requests), so the slate was confirmed from Wikipedia and a WHDH report of October 18 (the Secretary of the Commonwealth's candidate list, the WhereDoIVoteMA ballot pages and the elections-division pages return an Incapsula block from this machine, and the ElectionStats site only has results through the primary), The Green Papers (all three tickets, no others) that names the three tickets on the printed ballot (Healey/Driscoll, Minogue/Oliver, James/Kittredge). Gubernatorial candidates with no public footprint or who did not qualify are not included. Healey's record lists three signed bills; the Chapter 135 and 150 pages are the official session laws, and the gun-law description comes from AP coverage. No record items are listed for Minogue, described by the Boston.com primary report as a political newcomer. Andrea James's positions and priorities come from her campaign website's home and platform pages, which list headings rather than full policy papers. Oliver's arrest and charges come from The New Bedford Light and Boston.com, both fetched directly.
